Session 29: lme4 Model Criticism & Advanced Mixed-Effects Diagnostics

Research Data and Methods Workshop Series — Collaborative Research Centre (CRC 1252) ‘Prominence in Language’

Author

Job Schepens

Published

September 30, 2026

1 Introduction: Model Criticism in Quantitative Linguistics

Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMMs) and Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) fitted via lme4 (Bates, Mächler, et al. 2015) are the cornerstone of contemporary quantitative and experimental linguistics. They empower researchers to model hierarchically clustered data, handle unbalanced designs, and simultaneously account for variation across speakers and linguistic materials.

However, standard summary tables can easily mask fatal assumption violations. A model that converges without error may violate core Gauss-Markov assumptions, suffer from degenerate random-effects geometry (singularity), or be driven by a handful of influential participants or idiosyncratic stimulus items (Meteyard and Davies 2020).

NoteWorkshop Datasets: Authentic Linguistic Foundations for CRC 1252

Rather than generic non-linguistic toy examples (such as the sleepstudy, which lacks item variation and linguistic structure), this workshop demonstrates all diagnostic workflows on three authentic linguistic datasets:

  1. Continuous Reaction Time LMM (languageR::lexdec) (Baayen, Feldman, and Schreuder 2006): Visual lexical decision reaction times (\(N = 1,659\)) with crossed random factors (21 Subjects crossed with 79 Words), continuous linguistic predictors (Lexical Frequency, Word Length), participant background (NativeLanguage), and experimental progression (Trial).
  2. Discrete Syntactic Choice GLMM (languageR::dative) (Bresnan et al. 2007): Dative alternation choices (\(N = 3,263\); double object NP give John the book vs. prepositional PP give the book to John), directly testing prominence hierarchies central to CRC 1252 (Animacy, Pronominality, Givenness, End-Weight).
  3. Ordinal Subjective Rating CLMM (languageR::sizeRatings): Semantic size ratings (\(N = 3,078\)) on a 7-point Likert scale across 38 subjects and 81 concrete nouns, demonstrating why naive Gaussian models fail on bounded ordinal responses.

2 Methodological Landscape: A Decade of Mixed-Effects Developments (2014–2024+)

Over the past decade, mixed-effects modeling in experimental linguistics and psychology has undergone profound methodological advancements. Understanding these developments clarifies why contemporary model criticism goes far beyond legacy residual checks:

2.1 1. The Random-Effects Complexity Debate (2013–2017)

In a landmark paper, Barr et al. (2013) argued that confirmatory hypothesis testing requires “maximal” random-effects structures—including random intercepts and random slopes for all within-unit factors—to avoid Type I error rates soaring to 20–40%. However, Bates, Kliegl, et al. (2015) and Matuschek et al. (2017) demonstrated through extensive simulations that fitting maximal models on finite empirical datasets frequently produces overparameterization, severe loss of statistical power, and singular fits. They advocated for principled, data-driven model selection to strike an optimal balance between Type I error control and power.

2.2 2. The GLMM Residual Revolution: DHARMa (2016–2022)

For decades, researchers struggled to diagnose Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) because raw, Pearson, and deviance residuals fail catastrophically on discrete binary and count outcomes due to intrinsic mean-variance coupling. Florian Hartig (2022) solved this by introducing simulation-based quantile residuals using the Probability Integral Transform (PIT). This transformed GLMM diagnostics from an intractable guessing game into a rigorous testing suite for uniformity, overdispersion, and zero-inflation.

2.3 3. Ben Bolker’s Convergence Tooling & glmmTMB

As lead maintainer of lme4, Ben Bolker pioneered diagnostic tooling to demystify optimization warnings (Bolker et al. 2009). Key developments include: - lme4::allFit(): Benchmarking models across multiple derivative-free optimizers to detect false-positive convergence warnings. - lme4::isSingular(): Mathematical boundary checking based on Cholesky factor singular values. - glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017): Flexible template-model-builder architecture handling complex dispersion, zero-inflation, and spatial/temporal autocorrelation structures. - trouBBlme4SolveR: Automated diagnostic routines to resolve boundary singularities.

2.4 4. Unified Model Criticism via easystats (2020–2024)

The easystats ecosystem (Lüdecke et al. 2021) unified disparate diagnostic scripts into coherent workflows: - performance::check_model(): A comprehensive visual audit covering linearity, homoscedasticity, posterior predictive checks, collinearity, and random-effect normality. - performance::r2_nakagawa(): Formalized variance partitioning into Marginal and Conditional \(R^2\) (Nakagawa and Schielzeth 2013).

2.5 5. Post-Fitting & Marginal Effects (emmeans & marginaleffects)

Russell Lenth’s emmeans (2016) and Vincent Arel-Bundock’s marginaleffects (2024) established modern protocols for post-hoc contrasts, reference grids, and counterfactual prediction on the response scale.

2.6 6. The Bayesian Migration: brms (2017–2024)

Paul-Christian Bürkner’s brms (2017) opened full Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) estimation via Stan to applied linguists. As Vasishth et al. (2018) emphasize, weakly informative priors naturally regularize boundary estimates, eliminating frequentist singular fits without requiring researchers to discard scientifically motivated random slopes.

3 Comparative Assumptions Matrix: ANOVA vs. lme4 vs. brms

The table below summarizes how assumptions have evolved from classical ANOVA to modern Bayesian mixed models:

Assumption Dimension RM-ANOVA lme4 Linear (LMM) lme4 Generalized (GLMM) Bayesian Mixed Models (brms) Modern Diagnostic Tool
Design Balance Strict balance required; listwise deletion for missing cells Unbalanced cells and missing observations handled natively Unbalanced cells and missing observations handled natively Unbalanced cells and missing observations handled natively Missing data audits (naniar, summary)
Sphericity Required; violated sphericity inflates \(F\)-test Type I errors Relaxed: Variance-covariance components modeled directly Relaxed: Variance-covariance components modeled directly Relaxed: Full covariance prior (e.g. LKJ) modeled directly Mauchly’s test (ANOVA only; bypassed in mixed models)
Crossed Item Variation Violated: Language-as-fixed-effect fallacy (Clark 1973) Satisfied: Crossed random intercepts & slopes (Subject + Word) Satisfied: Crossed random structures Satisfied: Crossed random structures with regularizing priors Crossed formula syntax: (1 \| Subject) + (1 \| Word)
Residual Distribution \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) (Normality required) Uniform quantile residuals \(\mathcal{U}(0,1)\) via PIT Full posterior predictive distribution matching data family Q-Q plots, performance::check_model(), DHARMa::testUniformity()
Homoscedasticity Homogeneity across groups required Homoscedastic residual variance \(\sigma^2\) assumed Variance coupled to mean (\(\mu(1-\mu)\)); overdispersion fatal Can model residual variance as distributional regression (sigma ~ ...) Scale-location plots, DHARMa::testDispersion()
Linearity & Scaling Linear relationships assumed Linear on response scale; scale continuous predictors Linear on link scale (log, logit, probit, cloglog) Linear or non-linear on link scale Partial residual plots, check_model()
Random Effects Normality N/A BLUPs assumed multivariate normal: \(b \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)\) Conditional modes assumed multivariate normal Priors specify random-effects distributions (Normal, Student-\(t\)) Q-Q plots of BLUPs, check_model()
Singularity & Boundaries N/A Critical vulnerability: Boundary collapse (\(\sigma_b^2 = 0, \rho = \pm 1\)) Critical vulnerability: Laplace boundary failure Immune: Regularizing priors keep estimates off hard boundary lme4::isSingular(), trouBBlme4SolveR::dwmw()
Residual Independence Assumed across trials Assumed; sequential trial fatigue violates independence Assumed; temporal/spatial clustering violates independence Autoregressive structures can be added (ar(), cor_ar()) acf(), DHARMa::testTemporalAutocorrelation()

5 Module 1: Continuous Reaction Times & The Singularity Debate

5.1 1.1 Preparing Linguistic Lexical Decision Data & Random Effects Syntax

5.1.1 Random Effects Syntax Reference

Mixed-effects models relax the rigid balanced-design and sphericity assumptions of repeated-measures ANOVA: - Nested random effects (e.g., Students nested within Classrooms): Formula: (1 | Class / Student) or (1 | Class) + (1 | Class:Student) - Crossed random effects (e.g., Participants crossed with Stimulus Words): Formula: (1 | Subject) + (1 | Word)

We prepare languageR::lexdec (Baayen, Feldman, and Schreuder 2006), standardizing continuous predictors to optimize numerical conditioning and applying centered sum contrast coding (\(-0.5 / +0.5\)) to categorical factors (Schad et al. 2020):

Toggle Code 
# Load lexical decision dataset from languageR (Baayen et al., 2006)
data(lexdec)

# 1. Rescale continuous predictors to z-scores (mean = 0, sd = 1)
#    This eliminates scale disparities and avoids ill-conditioned deviance valleys
# 2. Apply centered sum contrast coding (-0.5 / +0.5) to two-level factors
#    Ensures intercept represents grand mean and beta represents true main effects
lexdec <- lexdec %>%
  mutate(
    Freq_z     = as.numeric(scale(Frequency)),
    Length_z   = as.numeric(scale(Length)),
    Native_num = ifelse(NativeLanguage == "Other", 0.5, -0.5),
    Sex_num    = ifelse(Sex == "M", 0.5, -0.5)
  )

# Inspect processed variables
glimpse(select(lexdec, Subject, Word, RT, Trial, Freq_z, Length_z, Native_num, Sex_num))

ImportantWhy Contrast Coding is Essential Before Model Fitting

In R, factors default to treatment (dummy) coding (contr.treatment), which maps the first alphabetical level to 0 and all other levels to 1. In mixed-effects modeling, this default creates three major hazards (Schad et al. 2020):

  1. Misinterpretation of Main Effects: In models with interactions (\(A \times B\)), the lower-order \(\beta\) coefficients under treatment coding are not main effects; they are simple effects restricted specifically to the arbitrary baseline level of the other factor.
  2. Artificial Random Slope Singularity: In (1 + Condition | Subject), treatment coding forces the random intercept to represent variance specifically at the baseline condition. This induces severe collinearity between the random intercept and random slope, driving the estimated correlation parameter \(\rho\) to boundary values of \(\pm 1.0\) and triggering false singular fits.
  3. Invalid Type III ANOVA Tables: Type III tests (car::Anova(type = "III")) mathematically assume orthogonal contrasts (contr.sum). Under default treatment coding, Type III tests are statistically meaningless.

Centered sum coding (\(-0.5 / +0.5\)) centers the intercept at the unweighted grand mean across conditions, decouples random intercepts from random slopes, and ensures \(\beta\) coefficients represent true main effects.

5.2 1.2 Fitting a Maximal Model (Barr et al., 2013)

According to Barr et al. (2013), any factor varying within a grouping unit must have a corresponding random slope: - Within Subject: Freq_z, Length_z - Within Word: Native_num, Sex_num

Toggle Code 
# Fit maximal random-effects model (Barr et al., 2013)
# Random intercepts and within-unit random slopes for all predictors:
# - Within Subject: Frequency and Word Length
# - Within Word: Native Language and Speaker Sex
m_maximal <- lmer(
  RT ~ Freq_z + Length_z + Native_num + Sex_num +
    (1 + Freq_z + Length_z | Subject) +
    (1 + Native_num + Sex_num | Word),
  data = lexdec
)

# Test for singularity (Cholesky factor on boundary)
cat("Is the maximal model singular?", isSingular(m_maximal), "\n")
Is the maximal model singular? TRUE

5.3 1.3 Inspecting Boundary Singularity

When isSingular() returns TRUE, the variance-covariance matrix lies on the boundary:

Toggle Code 
# Inspect estimated variance-covariance matrices and correlation parameters (rho)
# Look for variances collapsing to 0.000 or correlations at +/- 1.000
print(VarCorr(m_maximal))
 Groups   Name        Std.Dev. Corr          
 Word     (Intercept) 0.052691               
          Native_num  0.034874  0.760        
          Sex_num     0.017057 -0.799 -0.998 
 Subject  (Intercept) 0.142155               
          Freq_z      0.018883 -0.433        
          Length_z    0.023393  0.921 -0.473 
 Residual             0.168190
WarningDiagnostic Finding: Singularity Collapse

Notice that the Word random intercept standard deviation has collapsed to 0.000 with a boundary correlation of 1.000. The dataset cannot support estimating independent item-level slopes for speaker background factors alongside intercepts (Bates, Kliegl, et al. 2015).

5.4 1.4 Automated Singularity Resolution (trouBBlme4SolveR)

The trouBBlme4SolveR::dwmw() function diagnoses which random slope has zero variance and systematically prunes it:

Toggle Code 
# Automated troubleshooting for singular fits (Ben Bolker's trouBBlme4SolveR)
# 'dwmw' ("Don't Worry, Make Warmer") iteratively tests and prunes zero-variance random slopes
m_resolved <- dwmw(m_maximal)
cat("\nIs resolved model singular?", isSingular(m_resolved), "\n")

Is resolved model singular? FALSE

6 Module 2: Simulation Diagnostics with DHARMa

6.1 2.1 Classical Residual Checks in Linear Mixed Models

In standard Gaussian LMMs, residuals are assumed to follow \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\):

Toggle Code 
# Parsimonious random-effects model (Bates et al., 2015)
# Retains subject-level frequency slope; prunes overparameterized item slopes
m_parsimonious <- lmer(
  RT ~ Freq_z + Length_z + Native_num + (1 + Freq_z | Subject) + (1 | Word),
  data = lexdec
)
Toggle Code 
# Classical diagnostic plots for Gaussian LMM:
# Left: Normal Q-Q plot to assess residual normality (epsilon ~ N(0, sigma^2))
# Right: Residuals vs. Fitted to assess homoscedasticity and linearity
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(residuals(m_parsimonious), main = "Normal Q-Q Plot (Raw Residuals)")
qqline(residuals(m_parsimonious), col = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(fitted(m_parsimonious), residuals(m_parsimonious),
     xlab = "Fitted Values (log RT)", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs. Fitted", pch = 16, col = rgb(0,0,0,0.2))
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
Toggle Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

6.2 2.2 Discrete GLMM Residual Crisis & Probability Integral Transform

In discrete GLMMs (e.g. logistic regression), raw and Pearson residuals form parallel diagonal bands because outcomes are binary (\(y \in \{0, 1\}\)).

The DHARMa package (Hartig 2022) uses the Probability Integral Transform (PIT) to simulate \(n\) datasets from the fitted model and compute quantile residuals: \[u_i = P(Y^{\text{sim}}_i \le y_i) \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)\]

6.3 2.3 DHARMa in Action: Prominence in the Dative Alternation

We model the English dative alternation (Bresnan et al. 2007), where prominence features (animate recipients, pronominal recipients, short themes) predict the double-object construction (NP) versus prepositional construction (PP):

Toggle Code 
# Discrete Prominence GLMM: English Dative Alternation (Bresnan et al., 2007)
# Binary outcome: Realization of recipient as NP (double object) vs PP (prepositional)
data(dative)

m_dative <- glmer(
  RealizationOfRecipient ~ AnimacyOfRec + PronomOfRec + LengthOfTheme + (1 | Verb),
  family = binomial,
  data = dative
)
summary(m_dative)

6.4 2.4 Testing Sequential Autocorrelation across Trials

In self-paced reading and reaction time experiments, participant fatigue often induces temporal autocorrelation. We aggregate residuals across participants for each experimental trial:

Toggle Code 
# 1. Simulate residuals for continuous reaction time model
sim_lexdec <- simulateResiduals(fittedModel = m_parsimonious, n = 250, plot = FALSE)

# 2. Recalculate and aggregate residuals across subjects per experimental trial
# (Crucial: avoids non-unique time value error in repeated measures)
sim_trial <- recalculateResiduals(sim_lexdec, group = lexdec$Trial)

# 3. Formal Durbin-Watson / Moran's I test on aggregated trial time series
testTemporalAutocorrelation(sim_trial, time = unique(lexdec$Trial))

    Durbin-Watson test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals ~ 1
DW = 2.1971, p-value = 0.2068
alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is not 0
Toggle Code 
# 4. Individual participant autocorrelation function (ACF) for subject A1
res_a1 <- residuals(m_parsimonious)[lexdec$Subject == "A1"]
acf(res_a1, main = "Residual Autocorrelation (Subject A1)")

7 Module 3: Multicollinearity, Multi-Panel Checks & Cluster Influence

7.1 3.1 Multicollinearity & Variance Inflation Factors (VIF)

In natural language, lexical features naturally correlate (Zipf’s Law: frequent words are shorter). We test Variance Inflation Factors using performance::check_collinearity():

Toggle Code 
# Check multicollinearity using Variance Inflation Factors (VIF)
# VIF measures how much predictor variance is inflated due to collinearity with other predictors
# Rule of thumb: VIF < 5 is safe; VIF > 10 indicates severe collinearity
vif_results <- check_collinearity(m_parsimonious)
print(vif_results)

7.2 3.2 Unified Multi-Panel Diagnostics (easystats)

The performance::check_model() interface generates a comprehensive 6-panel diagnostic suite covering linearity, homoscedasticity, posterior predictive checks, normality of residuals, normality of random effects (BLUPs), and multicollinearity.

Toggle Code 
# Multi-panel model check from easystats:
# Generates 6 diagnostic panels: Linearity, Homoscedasticity, Posterior Predictive Checks,
# Residual Normality, BLUP Random Effect Normality, and Multicollinearity (VIF)
check_model(m_parsimonious)

7.3 3.3 Cluster-Level Influence & Cook’s Distance (influence.ME)

We check whether particular speakers or items exert disproportionate leverage (Nieuwenhuis, Grotenhuis, and Pelzer 2012):

Toggle Code 
# Subject-level Cook's Distance via iterative cluster deletion (influence.ME)
# Benchmark threshold for influential clusters: 4 / N_clusters
infl_subj <- influence(m_parsimonious, group = "Subject", count = FALSE)
plot(infl_subj, which = "cook", cutoff = 4 / length(unique(lexdec$Subject)),
     main = "Subject-Level Cook's Distance (lexdec)")
Toggle Code 
# Extract standardized parameter changes upon cluster deletion (DFBETAS)
# Measures how many standard errors each fixed effect moves when a subject is dropped

8 Module 4: Ordinal Responses & Cumulative Link Models

8.1 4.1 The Likert Assumption Fallacy

Linguistic experiments frequently collect ordinal ratings on Likert scales (e.g. acceptability, semantic size, prototypicality). A widespread practice is treating 1–7 Likert ratings as metric Gaussian variables via lme4::lmer().

This practice violates three fundamental assumptions: 1. Bounded Support: Data are bounded at 1 and 7 (floor/ceiling distortions). 2. Non-Interval Metric: The cognitive distance between “1” and “2” is not guaranteed to equal the distance between “4” and “5”. 3. Discrete Latent Thresholds: Responses reflect an underlying continuous latent variable \(Y^*\) partitioned by cutpoints \(\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \dots < \theta_{K-1}\).

8.2 4.2 Demonstrating the Flaw: Gaussian LMM on Likert Data

Using languageR::sizeRatings (3,078 size ratings of 81 words across 38 subjects on a 1–7 scale):

Toggle Code 
data(sizeRatings)

# 1. Naive Gaussian LMM: treating discrete 1-7 Likert ratings as metric Gaussian variable
m_naive_likert <- lmer(Rating ~ Class + (1 | Word), data = sizeRatings)

# 2. DHARMa diagnostic simulation: reveals severe floor/ceiling S-shaped quantile distortion
sim_naive <- simulateResiduals(m_naive_likert, n = 250, plot = FALSE)
plot(sim_naive)
CautionDiagnostic Warning: Severe Quantile Distortion

The DHARMa Q-Q plot on the naive Gaussian fit exhibits severe, statistically significant S-shaped curvature and failed uniformity tests (\(p < 10^{-16}\)), proving that standard Gaussian mixed models fail on bounded Likert data.

8.3 4.3 The Principled Solution: Cumulative Link Mixed Models (ordinal::clmm)

We fit a proper Cumulative Link Mixed Model using ordinal::clmm (Christensen 2019):

\[\text{logit}(P(Y_i \le k)) = \theta_k - (X_i \beta + Z_i u)\]

Toggle Code 
# Cumulative Link Mixed Model (Christensen, 2019)
# Convert ratings into an ordered factor (1 < 2 < ... < 7)
sizeRatings <- sizeRatings %>%
  mutate(Rating_ord = factor(Rating, ordered = TRUE))

# Fit CLMM: models cumulative log-odds with latent cutpoints (theta_1 to theta_6)
m_clmm <- clmm(Rating_ord ~ Class + (1 | Word), data = sizeRatings)
summary(m_clmm)

9.1 5.1 Estimating Marginal Means & Contrasts

The emmeans package (Lenth 2016) computes Estimated Marginal Means (least-squares means) by averaging predictions over a balanced reference grid:

9.2 5.2 Empirical Demonstration: Coding Invariance of emmeans

A profound property of emmeans is that it evaluates predictions over a balanced reference grid regardless of how factors were coded in the design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\).

Let us compare two identical models fitted with default treatment coding vs. centered sum coding:

Toggle Code 
# 1. Model fitted with default treatment (dummy) coding (English = 0, Other = 1)
m_treatment <- lmer(RT ~ Freq_z * NativeLanguage + (1 | Subject), data = lexdec)

# 2. Model fitted with centered sum contrast coding (-0.5 / +0.5)
m_sum <- lmer(RT ~ Freq_z * Native_num + (1 | Subject), data = lexdec)

# Comparison of Fixed Effects Tables:
# - In m_treatment: 'NativeLanguageOther' is a simple effect at Freq_z = 0
# - In m_sum: 'Native_num' is a true main effect averaged across all words
cat("=== Fixed Effects under Treatment Coding ===\n")

9.3 5.3 Methodological Assumptions of emmeans

When reporting marginal means, researchers must verify five underlying assumptions:

  1. Reference Grid Balancing: Continuous covariates are held constant at their grand mean (\(\bar{x}\)), and factor cells are weighted equally. When covariates are correlated, the reference grid can evaluate combinations unobserved in actual data.
  2. Scale of Inference: Differences on the link scale (log-odds) back-transform to odds ratios or ratio of medians on the response scale.
  3. Degrees of Freedom Approximations: For LMMs, emmeans supports Kenward-Roger and Satterthwaite approximations (Kuznetsova, Brockhoff, and Christensen 2017). Kenward-Roger is preferred in unbalanced crossed designs to avoid anticonservative tests.
  4. Homoscedasticity & Pooled Variance: Standard errors in emmeans assume a shared residual variance \(\sigma^2\) across factor levels.
  5. Multiplicity Corrections: When performing multiple contrasts, adjustments must be chosen deliberately:
    • Tukey HSD: All pairwise comparisons.
    • Bonferroni / Šidák: Planned orthogonal contrasts.
    • Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR): Large exploratory contrast families.

9.4 5.4 Why Both Are Necessary: The Two-Stage Principle

If emmeans produces the same marginal means regardless of factor coding, why do we still need contrast coding before fitting? Conversely, if we use sum contrast coding, why do we still need emmeans?

The answer lies in the distinction between model estimation (a priori) and hypothesis evaluation (post hoc):

Dimension / Objective Contrast Coding (Before Fitting) emmeans (After Fitting) Why Both Are Essential
Operational Stage A priori: Parameterizes the design matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) during numerical optimization. Post hoc: Constructs reference grid predictions from estimated \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}\). Neither tool can perform the other’s job: emmeans cannot refit the model; contrast coding cannot predict across balanced grids automatically.
Random Slope Stability Crucial: Centered coding centers random intercepts at the grand mean, preventing artificial correlation collapse (\(\rho \approx \pm 1.0\)) and singular fits. Cannot help: Operates only on the already-converged model. If uncentered coding triggered a singular fit, emmeans cannot repair the corrupted variance parameters. You must contrast-code before fitting to ensure the model converges to valid, non-singular variance estimates.
Coefficient Interpretation Ensures lower-order \(\beta\) terms in summary() represent true main effects rather than simple effects at an arbitrary baseline. Does not alter the \(\beta\) regression table; only provides reconstructed marginal predictions. Researchers reading model tables require interpretable \(\beta\) coefficients for regression reporting.
Type III ANOVA (car::Anova) Strictly Required: Type III tests mathematically assume sum/orthogonal contrasts (contr.sum). Under treatment coding, Type III tests are statistically meaningless. Not applicable (evaluates specific linear contrasts rather than overall omnibus decomposition). If journal reviewers demand Type III Wald/LRT ANOVA tables, models must be fitted with sum contrasts.
Interaction Decomposition Slicing interactions via contrast matrices requires tedious manual coding of custom linear combinations (\(\mathbf{c}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}\)) or repeatedly releveling baselines. Trivial: Syntax like pairwise ~ FactorA \| FactorB decomposes multi-way interactions into simple pairwise differences in a single line. You need emmeans to explore interactions cleanly without refitting the model multiple times.
Response Scale for GLMMs Operates strictly on the link scale (log-odds \(\eta\)). Back-transforming manually requires tedious delta-method calculations for SEs. Native: Converts log-odds to response probabilities (\(p \in [0, 1]\)) and odds ratios with automatic multivariate delta-method standard errors. You need emmeans to translate abstract log-odds coefficients into meaningful probabilities for publication.
Multiplicity & d.f. Corrections Manual adjustment of \(p\)-values and manual calculation of Satterthwaite/Kenward-Roger d.f. Automated integration with lmerTest/pbkrtest for Satterthwaite/Kenward-Roger d.f. and Tukey/FDR adjustments. You need emmeans to avoid anticonservative inferential tests.
TipThe Gold-Standard Two-Stage Workflow
  1. Stage 1 (Before Model Fitting): Apply centered sum contrast coding (contr.sum or \(-0.5 / +0.5\)) to all categorical predictors. This stabilizes the random-effects covariance matrix against boundary singularities, aligns \(\beta\) coefficients with main effects, and validates Type III ANOVA tables.
  2. Stage 2 (After Model Fitting): Use emmeans to evaluate condition means across balanced reference grids, unpack complex interactions, compute response-scale probabilities and odds ratios, and apply Kenward-Roger d.f. approximations and Tukey multiplicity adjustments.

10.2 6.2 Likelihood Ratio Tests: Enforcing REML vs. ML Rules

  • Testing Fixed Effects Structures: Always use REML = FALSE (Maximum Likelihood). REML likelihoods depend on fixed-effect design matrices, making LRTs under REML mathematically invalid.
  • Testing Random Effects Structures: Use REML = TRUE with anova(m1, m2).
  • Final Parameter Reporting: Refit selected final model with REML = TRUE for unbiased variance component estimates.
Toggle Code 
# Nested model comparison for fixed effect of Frequency under Maximum Likelihood (REML = FALSE)
m_full_ml <- lmer(RT ~ Freq_z + Length_z + Native_num + (1 | Subject) + (1 | Word),
                  data = lexdec, REML = FALSE)
m_null_ml <- lmer(RT ~ Length_z + Native_num + (1 | Subject) + (1 | Word),
                  data = lexdec, REML = FALSE)

# Likelihood Ratio Test (Chisq test on deviance difference)
anova(m_null_ml, m_full_ml)

10.3 6.3 Variance Partitioning: Nakagawa’s \(R^2\)

For mixed models, standard \(R^2\) does not apply. Nakagawa & Schielzeth (2013) partition variance into: - Marginal \(R^2_m\): Proportion of variance explained by fixed effects alone. - Conditional \(R^2_c\): Proportion of variance explained by both fixed and random effects (total model variance).

Toggle Code 
# Compute Nakagawa Marginal (R2m) and Conditional (R2c) R-squared metrics
r2_metrics <- r2_nakagawa(m_resolved)
Random effect variances not available. Returned R2 does not account for random effects.
Toggle Code 
print(r2_metrics)
# R2 for Mixed Models

  Conditional R2: NA
     Marginal R2: 0.126

10.4 6.4 Open Science Reporting Checklist (Meteyard and Davies 2020)

  1. Specification: State full formula syntax, contrast coding schemes, and scaling transformations.
  2. Estimation: Specify REML vs. ML, optimizer choice, and integration method.
  3. Diagnostics: Report isSingular() checks, DHARMa dispersion/uniformity tests, and VIF metrics.
  4. Parameters: Provide fixed effect estimates (\(\beta\), \(SE\), \(t/z\), df approximation, \(p\)), random effect variance components (\(\sigma, \rho\)), and Nakagawa \(R^2\) (\(R^2_m, R^2_c\)).
  5. Reproducibility: Share annotated Quarto (.qmd) scripts and data in open repositories.
